theory_mcq.question: What does LIFO stand for, and how does it define a stack's behavior?
options: Last In First Out — the most recently added element is the first one removed
Last In Final Order — elements are removed in the order they were declared
Linear Input First Output — elements are processed in array index order
Limited Input For Output — a stack can only hold a fixed number of elements
theory_mcq.explanation: LIFO (Last In First Out) is the defining property of a stack: whatever was pushed most recently is always the first thing popped — this is the core behavioral contract that distinguishes a stack from other data structures like a queue.

theory_mcq.question: Why are push and pop both O(1) operations when implemented using the END of a JavaScript array, but NOT when implemented using the FRONT of the array?
options: There's no actual difference; both ends perform identically

Operating at the END of an array requires no shifting of other elements (nothing comes after the last position), while operating at the FRONT requires shifting every other element by one position to maintain contiguity — this is the same array-operation asymmetry covered in L1-M02
JavaScript arrays only support operations at the end, never at the front
Front operations are O(1) while end operations are O(n)
theory_mcq.explanation: This directly applies the L1-M02 principle: end-of-array operations (push/pop) don't require shifting since nothing follows the last element, while front-of-array operations (shift/unshift) require shifting every other element — exactly why the lesson explicitly warns against using shift()/unshift() for stack operations.

theory_mcq.question: Why is the OS-level function call stack a natural real-world example of the stack data structure?
options: Because function calls have nothing to do with stacks

Because function calls follow LIFO: when function A calls function B, B must completely finish (return) before A can resume — the most recently called function is always the first to return, exactly matching the stack's LIFO property, as covered in L1-M01's recursion lesson
Because the call stack is implemented using a queue internally
Because functions are called in alphabetical order
theory_mcq.explanation: This connects directly to L1-M01's recursion lesson: when functions call other functions, the most recently called function must complete and return before control passes back to its caller — this LIFO completion order is precisely why the call stack is called a 'stack' and behaves identically to the LIFO data structure covered here.

theory_mcq.question: What does a 'stack overflow' mean at the hardware/runtime level?
options: It means the stack data structure contains too many duplicate values

It means the call stack (or any stack-based memory region) has exceeded its allocated memory capacity — typically from excessive or unbounded recursion (each call adding a frame without returning), causing the program to crash since there's no more space to push additional frames
It refers to a stack array exceeding JavaScript's maximum array length
It only happens when using array-based stacks, never linked-list-based ones
theory_mcq.explanation: A stack overflow occurs when more is pushed onto a stack-based memory region than it has capacity for — most commonly from runaway recursion (as covered in L1-M01: a missing base case causes indefinite stack frame pushes), eventually exhausting the memory reserved for the call stack and crashing the program.

logic_mcq.question: Trace the browser history example: `visit('home'); visit('about'); visit('courses'); goBack();` then `currentPage()`. What does currentPage() return, and why?
options: 'courses' — goBack() doesn't actually change the current page
'about' — visit() pushes each page (history becomes ['home','about','courses']), goBack() pops the top ('courses') leaving ['home','about'], so the new top (currentPage()) is 'about'
'home' — goBack() always returns to the very first page
undefined — the history stack is empty after goBack()
logic_mcq.explanation: Tracing the stack operations exactly: three visit() calls push 'home', 'about', 'courses' (top is 'courses'). goBack() pops 'courses' (since history.length > 1), leaving ['home','about'] with 'about' now at the top — so currentPage() (which reads the top without removing it) returns 'about'.

logic_mcq.question: In the `goBack()` function, why does it check `history.length > 1` rather than `history.length > 0` before popping?
options: This is an arbitrary choice with no functional purpose

Requiring length > 1 (rather than > 0) prevents popping the very LAST remaining page, ensuring there's always at least one page left to be the 'current' page — if length were only checked against 0, goBack() could empty the entire history, leaving no current page to display
JavaScript arrays cannot have a length of exactly 1
This check has no effect; the condition could be removed without changing behavior
logic_mcq.explanation: This is a deliberate safety guard: if the stack only had length > 0 as the condition, calling goBack() when only one page remains (e.g., just ['home']) would pop it, leaving an EMPTY history with no current page — requiring length > 1 ensures at least one page always remains, so currentPage() never fails on an empty stack.

syntax_mcq.question: In `stack[stack.length - 1]`, why is `stack.length - 1` used to access the 'top' of the stack, rather than `stack[0]`?
options: stack[0] would actually be correct; this is unnecessarily complex

Since push/pop operate at the END of the array (for O(1) performance), the 'top' of the stack — the most recently added element — is located at the LAST index of the array, which is stack.length - 1 (since array indices are zero-based, the last valid index is always one less than the length)
stack.length - 1 always evaluates to 0
This syntax only works for arrays with exactly one element
syntax_mcq.explanation: Because push() and pop() operate at the array's end for O(1) performance, the most-recently-pushed element (the LIFO 'top') sits at the last index. Since arrays are zero-indexed, the last valid index is always `length - 1` — this is the standard idiom for peeking at an array-backed stack's top without removing it.

coding_challenges.title: Build a Browser History Manager with Forward/Back Navigation
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Extend the lesson's browser history pattern into a full navigation manager supporting both back AND forward navigation (visiting a new page after going back should clear any 'forward' history, matching real browser behavior).
requirements: Implement `BrowserHistory` class with `visit(page)`, `back()` (returns the page navigated to, or null if already at the oldest page), `forward()` (returns the page navigated to, or null if already at the newest page), and `current()` returning the current page
Visiting a new page after going back should DISCARD any forward history (matching real browsers: you can't go forward after navigating somewhere new from a back state)
All core navigation operations should be O(1)

test_cases.input: (() => { const b = new BrowserHistory('home'); b.visit('about'); return b.current(); })()
(() => { const b = new BrowserHistory('home'); b.visit('about'); b.visit('courses'); return b.back(); })()
(() => { const b = new BrowserHistory('home'); return b.back(); })()
(() => { const b = new BrowserHistory('home'); b.visit('about'); b.back(); b.visit('contact'); return b.forward(); })()
(() => { const b = new BrowserHistory('home'); b.visit('a'); b.visit('b'); b.back(); return b.forward(); })()

coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: visit: O(k) where k is the discarded forward history length (amortized O(1) when navigating forward normally, since slice only does work when forward history exists to discard). back/forward/current: O(1).

hints.text: Track both the history list AND a 'current position' index, rather than just a simple stack — this lets you support both back and forward.
visit(page): truncate the history to everything up to and including the current position, THEN append the new page and advance the index — this is what discards forward history.
back()/forward(): simply move the current index by one (if possible) and return the page at that new position.

theory_mcq.question: What is the key trade-off between an array-backed stack and a linked-list-backed stack?
options: There is no real trade-off; they perform identically in every situation

An array-backed stack is simple and cache-friendly with amortized O(1) operations (due to occasional resizing), while a linked-list-backed stack offers GUARANTEED O(1) operations with no resizing ever, at the cost of extra per-node memory overhead (storing pointers) and worse cache locality (nodes scattered in memory)
Linked-list-backed stacks are always faster in every benchmark
Array-backed stacks cannot support a peek() operation
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the core trade-off the lesson presents: array-backed offers simplicity and good cache locality but amortized (not guaranteed) O(1) due to occasional resize operations; linked-list-backed offers TRUE guaranteed O(1) per operation (no resizing needed) but pays a memory overhead cost for storing next-pointers and loses the cache-locality benefit of contiguous memory.

theory_mcq.question: In `LinkedStack`, why does `push(val)` create the new node with `new ListNode(val, this._top)` — passing the CURRENT top as the new node's `next` pointer — rather than appending the new node somewhere else?
options: This is incorrect; nodes should be appended at the list's end

Since the stack's 'top' must always be O(1) to access, the newest element needs to become the new head/top of the linked list immediately — by setting the new node's `next` to point to the OLD top, the new node becomes the new top while still correctly linking back to the rest of the stack's elements in their original LIFO order
This pointer assignment has no functional purpose and is purely stylistic
It creates a circular reference that would cause an infinite loop
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the core mechanism for O(1) linked-list stack operations: by making the new node point to the OLD top and then updating `this._top` to be the new node, the new node becomes the head of the list in O(1) — no traversal needed, since you're always inserting/removing at the very front (the head), which is exactly where `this._top` always points.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `testStack(LinkedStack)`: push(1), push(2), push(3), then pop(). What is `this._top.val` immediately after the pop() call completes?
options: 3, since pop() doesn't actually change the top

2 — push(1) makes top={val:1,next:null}; push(2) makes top={val:2,next:{val:1}}; push(3) makes top={val:3,next:{val:2,next:{val:1}}}; pop() reads val=3 to return, then sets this._top = this._top.next (the node holding val=2), making the new top's val equal to 2
1, since pop() always reverts to the first-pushed element
undefined, since the stack becomes empty after one pop
logic_mcq.explanation: Tracing the linked structure precisely: after three pushes, the chain is 3->2->1 (top to bottom). pop() captures the top's value (3) to return, then advances `this._top` to `this._top.next` — which is the node holding val=2 — making 2 the new top, consistent with LIFO behavior (most recently pushed, 3, is removed first).

logic_mcq.question: In `testStack`, after `s.pop()` is called enough times to empty the stack, calling `s.pop()` one more time returns `undefined` rather than throwing an error. Why does this matter for a stack implementation?
options: It doesn't matter; throwing an error would be equally acceptable

Safely handling an empty-stack pop (returning undefined rather than crashing) is an important defensive design choice — many algorithms that use a stack internally (like Valid Parentheses, covered in L3) rely on checking the stack's emptiness BEFORE popping, but a safe pop() that doesn't crash provides an additional layer of robustness against bugs in calling code
JavaScript arrays always throw an error when popping an empty array, so this behavior is impossible to achieve
This behavior only applies to ArrayStack, not LinkedStack
logic_mcq.explanation: Both ArrayStack (via JS array.pop() returning undefined on empty) and LinkedStack (via the explicit `if (!this._top) return undefined;` guard) are designed to fail safely rather than throwing — this defensive behavior is valuable since many real algorithms (like the upcoming Valid Parentheses lesson) need to interact with potentially-empty stacks, and crash-free behavior on edge cases reduces the surface area for bugs.

logic_mcq.question: Both `testStack(ArrayStack)` and `testStack(LinkedStack)` are called with the exact same sequence of operations and produce IDENTICAL printed output. What does this demonstrate about the relationship between the two implementations?
options: It demonstrates that the two implementations are literally the same code

It demonstrates that ArrayStack and LinkedStack are BEHAVIORALLY EQUIVALENT — they expose the same external interface (push, pop, peek, isEmpty, size) and produce identical observable results for identical operations, even though their INTERNAL implementations (contiguous array vs. linked nodes) are completely different
It demonstrates that LinkedStack is actually broken and just copies ArrayStack's output
It demonstrates that stacks cannot have more than one valid implementation
logic_mcq.explanation: This is a demonstration of interface-implementation separation: both classes expose an identical PUBLIC API (push/pop/peek/isEmpty/size) and are interchangeable from the caller's perspective, even though their internal data representations (contiguous array vs. linked list of nodes) are entirely different — this is exactly why `testStack` can accept either class as a parameter and test both uniformly.

syntax_mcq.question: In `get size() { return this._data.length; }`, what does the `get` keyword accomplish here?
options: It defines a regular method that must be called as size()

It defines a GETTER — a special method that's accessed like a PROPERTY (s.size) rather than called like a function (s.size()), allowing `size` to be read with simple property-access syntax while still executing custom logic behind the scenes
It makes the size property read-write instead of read-only
get has no special meaning in this context; it's just a naming convention
syntax_mcq.explanation: The `get` keyword defines a getter accessor: callers access it as `stackInstance.size` (no parentheses, like a plain property) rather than `stackInstance.size()` (like a method call) — this is exactly how the lesson's testStack function uses `console.log(s.size)` without calling it as a function.

coding_challenges.title: Implement and Cross-Verify Array-Backed and Linked-List-Backed Stacks
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Implement both stack backing strategies from this lesson, then write an automated cross-verification tool that runs the SAME sequence of random operations against both implementations and confirms they always produce identical results.
requirements: Implement `ArrayStack` and `LinkedStack` (with `ListNode`) matching the lesson exactly

Implement `crossVerify(operations)` taking an array of operation descriptors (e.g., [{op:'push',val:5}, {op:'pop'}, {op:'peek'}]) and running them in sequence against BOTH stack types, returning true if every single operation produced the SAME result on both implementations throughout the entire sequence

test_cases.input: (() => { const s = new LinkedStack(); s.push(1); s.push(2); return s.peek(); })()
(() => { const s = new LinkedStack(); s.push(1); s.push(2); s.pop(); return s.size; })()

coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: ArrayStack operations: O(1) amortized. LinkedStack operations: O(1) guaranteed. crossVerify: O(m) where m is the number of operations, since each operation is O(1) on both implementations.

hints.text: LinkedStack.push: create a new node whose 'next' points to the current top, then make that new node the top, and increment size.
LinkedStack.pop: handle the empty case first (return undefined), otherwise capture the top's value, advance top to top.next, decrement size, and return the captured value.
crossVerify: maintain one instance of each stack type, apply each operation to BOTH, and compare their results at every single step — return false immediately on any mismatch.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson state that 'greedy or counting approaches fail for mixed bracket types', and what does a stack provide that counting doesn't?
options: Counting approaches always work fine; this claim is incorrect

A simple counter could verify EQUAL NUMBERS of opening and closing brackets overall, but it cannot verify CORRECT NESTING/ORDER — for example, '([)]' has equal counts of each bracket type but is invalid because brackets close in the wrong order; a stack tracks the exact ORDER openers were seen, allowing it to detect mismatched closing order, which counting cannot do
Counting approaches only work for a single type of bracket, never mixed types
A stack and a counter are functionally identical for this problem
theory_mcq.explanation: This is exactly the lesson's '([)]' trace example: a counting approach would see 2 opens and 2 closes (counts match) but miss that ')' incorrectly closes a '[' that's still open — only a stack, which preserves the ORDER of unclosed openers, can detect this kind of nesting violation.

theory_mcq.question: What are the THREE distinct failure conditions the lesson identifies for `isValid(s)`?
options: The string is too long; the string is empty; the string contains numbers

A closing bracket doesn't match the most recent unclosed opener (wrong closer); some openers are never closed by the end of the string (leftover openers); a closing bracket appears when the stack is already empty (closing with nothing open)
There is only ONE failure condition: unequal bracket counts
The brackets are in the wrong color
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's code explicitly checks for these three distinct failure modes: 'stack.length === 0 || stack[top] !== pairs[c]' inside the loop catches both 'closing empty stack' and 'wrong closer', and the final 'return stack.length === 0' check catches 'leftover openers' (unclosed brackets remaining at the end).

logic_mcq.question: Trace `isValid('({[]})')` per the lesson's own worked example. What is the final stack state, and what does isValid return?
options: Final stack: ['('], returns false
Final stack: [] (empty) after all three closers correctly match and pop their corresponding openers in reverse order, so isValid returns true
The function throws an error partway through
Final stack: ['(','{','['], returns false since nothing was ever popped
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: '(','{','[' are pushed in order (stack: ['(','{','[']), then ']','}',')']  each correctly match and pop the most recent unmatched opener in reverse order, leaving the stack empty at the end — so isValid returns true (stack.length === 0).

logic_mcq.question: Trace `isValid('([)]')` per the lesson's own worked example. At exactly which character does the function detect failure, and why?
options: It detects failure at the very first character '('

It detects failure at the third character ')' — at that point, stack=['(','['] (top is '['), but pairs[')'] expects '(' as the matching opener; since the actual top ('[') doesn't match the expected opener ('('), this is a MISMATCH, and the function returns false immediately
It never detects failure; this string is actually valid
It detects failure at the very last character ']'
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: after pushing '(' and '[' (stack=['(','[']), the third character ')' expects its matching opener to be '(' (per the pairs map), but the actual stack top is '[' — this MISMATCH (wrong opener at the top) triggers an immediate `return false`, without needing to process the remaining characters.

logic_mcq.question: In `validateTags`, why does the check `stack.pop() !== tag` need to happen specifically when encountering a CLOSING tag, and what does a true result from this comparison indicate?
options: This check happens for opening tags, not closing tags

When a closing tag (like '') is encountered, the function pops the most recently pushed (unclosed) opening tag and checks whether it matches the CURRENT closing tag's name — if they DON'T match (`!== tag` is true), it means tags are improperly nested (e.g., '

' tries to close 'div' while 'p' is still the most recently unclosed tag), so the function correctly returns false
This check verifies that the tag name is spelled correctly
This check has no functional purpose in the validation logic
logic_mcq.explanation:
This mirrors the bracket-matching logic exactly, generalized to tag names: popping the stack reveals the most recently opened (and not yet closed) tag, and the current closing tag must match that EXACT tag for correct nesting — a mismatch (popped tag !== current closing tag) signals improperly nested/overlapping tags, exactly the bug shown in the lesson's '

' example.

syntax_mcq.question: What does the object `{ ')': '(', '}': '{', ']': '[' }` represent and how is it used in `isValid`?
options: It's a list of all valid bracket characters with no other meaning

It's a lookup map from each CLOSING bracket character to its expected matching OPENING bracket character — used as `pairs[c]` when c is a closing bracket, to determine what opener SHOULD be at the top of the stack for a valid match
It converts closing brackets into their ASCII codes
It defines the order in which brackets must appear in the output
syntax_mcq.explanation: This object serves as a reverse lookup: given a closing bracket character (the key), it returns the SPECIFIC opening bracket character that's expected to match it (the value) — this is what allows the comparison `stack[stack.length-1] !== pairs[c]` to verify the correct opener is on top of the stack.

coding_challenges.title: Generalized Bracket and Tag Validator
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Implement Valid Parentheses and the generalized tag-validation pattern, then extend it to a configurable validator that can handle ANY set of opener-closer pairs (not just the three standard bracket types), demonstrating the pattern's full generality.
requirements: Implement `isValidImpl(s)` matching the lesson's bracket-matching approach exactly for '()', '{}', '[]'
Implement `validateTagsImpl(html)` matching the lesson's regex-based tag validation approach exactly

Implement `validateCustomPairs(s, pairMap)` generalizing isValidImpl to accept ANY opener-closer mapping (e.g., {'<':'>'}), where pairMap is an object mapping CLOSERS to their expected OPENERS, and s contains ONLY characters that are either openers, closers, or should be ignored (treat any character not in pairMap's keys or values as ignorable, simply skipping over it)
coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: isValidImpl: O(n) time, O(n) space. validateTagsImpl: O(n) time (regex scan plus stack operations), O(n) space. validateCustomPairs: O(n) time, O(n) space — generalizes the same pattern to arbitrary pair definitions.

hints.text: isValidImpl and validateTagsImpl should match the lesson's implementations exactly.
validateCustomPairs: build a Set of valid openers (values of pairMap) and a Set of valid closers (keys of pairMap) for quick membership checks.
For each character: if it's an opener, push it; if it's a closer, check the stack top matches pairMap[c] before popping; otherwise (any other character), simply skip it without affecting the stack.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the naive approach to getMin() (scanning all elements) fail to meet the O(1) requirement, and what does the auxiliary min-stack solve?
options: The naive approach is actually O(1); there's no real problem to solve

Scanning the entire stack to find the minimum is O(n) — proportional to the stack's size — which violates the O(1) requirement; the auxiliary min-stack solves this by maintaining a PARALLEL stack that tracks the minimum value at EVERY depth, so retrieving the current minimum is always just reading the top of this auxiliary stack, an O(1) operation
The auxiliary stack makes getMin() slower, not faster
There is no way to achieve O(1) getMin(); this is a misconception
theory_mcq.explanation: A naive scan-all-elements approach is O(n) since the work scales with stack size. The auxiliary min-stack trades extra space (storing a parallel running-minimum at every depth) for guaranteed O(1) time on getMin(), since the answer is always immediately available at the top of the auxiliary stack — no scanning required.

theory_mcq.question: Why must the auxiliary min-stack in `MinStack` push a value on EVERY single push to the main stack — not just when a NEW minimum is found?
options: This is unnecessary; pushing only on new minimums would also work correctly

If the auxiliary stack only pushed on new minimums, then after popping past a recent non-minimum element, the two stacks would become DESYNCHRONIZED (different lengths/depths) — pushing a value (either the new minimum OR the existing minimum, whichever is smaller) on EVERY push keeps both stacks the SAME SIZE at all times, ensuring pop() can safely remove from both in lockstep without losing track of what the minimum was at any given depth
Pushing on every operation makes the algorithm run faster
JavaScript requires both stacks to always have identical lengths or it throws an error
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the key correctness insight for the BASIC MinStack version (distinct from the Optimised variant): keeping both stacks synchronized in SIZE at every depth is what allows a simple `pop()` to remove from both stacks together and have the auxiliary stack's new top correctly reflect the minimum at the now-current depth — if the aux stack only tracked NEW minimums, popping the main stack wouldn't reliably tell you which aux entry corresponds to the new top.

logic_mcq.question: Trace the lesson's exact sequence on `MinStack`: push(5), push(3), push(7), push(2). What is `_minStack` after all four pushes?
options: [5, 5, 5, 5] — the minStack never changes after the first push

[5, 3, 3, 2] — push(5): min=5 (first element); push(3): min(3,5)=3; push(7): min(7,3)=3 (7 is not smaller); push(2): min(2,3)=2 — at each step, _minStack records the minimum of all elements pushed SO FAR
[5, 3, 7, 2] — minStack always mirrors the main stack exactly
[2, 2, 2, 2] — minStack only stores the global minimum repeated
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: 'push(5): minStack=[5]... push(3): minStack=[5,3] (min(3,5)=3)... push(7): minStack=[5,3,3] (min(7,3)=3)... push(2): minStack=[5,3,3,2] (min(2,3)=2)' — each entry in minStack is the running minimum of all elements pushed up to that point.

logic_mcq.question: Continuing the same trace, after `pop()` is called once (removing the most recently pushed element, 2), what does `getMin()` return, and why?
options: 2, since the minimum never changes once set

3 — pop() removes from BOTH stacks together: main stack becomes [5,3,7], minStack becomes [5,3,3] (the last entry, 2, is removed); getMin() reads the new top of minStack, which is 3 — correctly reflecting that with element 2 now removed, 3 is once again the minimum of the remaining elements
5, since pop() always reverts to the very first minimum
undefined, since pop() breaks the minStack tracking
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: 'pop(): stack=[5,3,7], minStack=[5,3,3]... getMin() -> minStack.top = 3 O(1) — correctly restored after pop' — popping both stacks together ensures minStack's new top always correctly reflects the minimum of whatever remains in the main stack.

logic_mcq.question: In `MinStackOptimised`, why does `pop()` check `if (val === this._minStack[top])` before deciding whether to pop the auxiliary stack, rather than always popping it like the basic MinStack does?
options: This check is unnecessary and could be removed

Since the optimized auxiliary stack only contains entries for values that WERE a new minimum (or tied) at the time they were pushed, popping it should only happen when the value being removed from the MAIN stack actually corresponds to the value at the TOP of the auxiliary stack — if the popped main-stack value isn't the current minimum, the auxiliary stack's top is unaffected and must NOT be popped, since the two stacks are no longer kept at the same size by design
This check always evaluates to true, making the condition pointless
The optimized version doesn't actually use an auxiliary stack at all
logic_mcq.explanation: Unlike the basic MinStack (which keeps both stacks synchronized in size by pushing on every operation), the optimized version's auxiliary stack only grows when a new minimum (or tie) occurs — so on pop(), it must check whether the value just removed from the MAIN stack matches the auxiliary stack's current top; only then does the auxiliary stack need to pop too, since that means the just-removed value WAS the tracked minimum.

syntax_mcq.question: In `const currentMin = this._minStack.length === 0 ? val : Math.min(val, this._minStack[this._minStack.length - 1]);`, what does this ternary expression compute?
options: It always returns val regardless of the minStack's state

If the auxiliary minStack is currently empty (this is the very first push), currentMin is simply val (since there's nothing to compare against yet); otherwise, currentMin is the smaller of val and the EXISTING minimum (the current top of minStack) — correctly handling both the 'first element' edge case and the general 'compare new value to running minimum' case in one expression
It always returns the existing minimum, ignoring the new value
It computes the maximum, not the minimum
syntax_mcq.explanation: This ternary handles two cases in one line: the empty-minStack edge case (first push ever, so the new value IS the minimum by default) versus the general case (compare the new value against whatever the running minimum currently is, keeping whichever is smaller) — this is the core logic that maintains a correct running minimum at every depth.

coding_challenges.title: Implement Both MinStack Variants and Verify Equivalence
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Implement both the basic and space-optimized MinStack variants from this lesson, then build a randomized stress test that runs identical operation sequences against both and confirms they always report the same getMin() result, despite their auxiliary stacks having potentially different internal sizes.
requirements: Implement `MinStack` matching the lesson's basic (push-on-every-push) approach exactly
Implement `MinStackOptimised` matching the lesson's space-optimized (push-only-on-new-min) approach exactly

Implement `stressTestEquivalence(operations)` that runs a sequence of {op:'push',val} / {op:'pop'} / {op:'getMin'} operations against BOTH variants, returning true only if every getMin() call produces IDENTICAL results on both

test_cases.input: (() => { const m = new MinStack(); m.push(5); m.push(3); m.push(7); m.push(2); return m.getMin(); })()
(() => { const m = new MinStack(); m.push(5); m.push(3); m.push(7); m.push(2); m.pop(); return m.getMin(); })()
(() => { const m = new MinStackOptimised(); m.push(5); m.push(3); m.push(7); m.push(2); return m.getMin(); })()

coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: MinStack: O(1) push/pop/getMin, O(n) auxiliary space (always synchronized in size with main stack). MinStackOptimised: O(1) push/pop/getMin, O(n) WORST-CASE auxiliary space but typically much smaller in practice (only grows on new minimums/ties). stressTestEquivalence: O(m) for m operations.

hints.text: MinStack.push: compute currentMin as either val (if minStack is empty) or the smaller of val and the existing top of minStack, then push currentMin.

MinStackOptimised.push: only push val to minStack if it's empty OR val is less than or equal to the current minStack top; pop: only pop minStack if the value removed from the main stack matches minStack's current top.
stressTestEquivalence: maintain one instance of each class, apply each operation to both in lockstep, and specifically compare getMin() results whenever that operation occurs in the sequence.

theory_mcq.question: What does FIFO stand for, and how does it differ from the LIFO property of a stack?
options: First In First Out — the FIRST element added is the FIRST one removed, which is the OPPOSITE order from a stack's LIFO (where the LAST element added is the FIRST removed)
FIFO is just another name for LIFO; they describe identical behavior
Final In First Out — elements are processed based on their final state
First In Final Out — only the last element added is ever processed
theory_mcq.explanation: FIFO (First In First Out) is the direct conceptual opposite of LIFO: a queue processes elements in the SAME order they were added (oldest first), while a stack processes them in REVERSE order (newest first) — this fundamental difference is what makes each structure suited to different problem classes.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson explicitly warn against using `arr.shift()` for queue dequeue operations on large queues?
options: shift() doesn't actually remove elements from the front

shift() removes the first element AND shifts every remaining element one position to the left to fill the gap — this is an O(n) operation, meaning dequeue would cost O(n) instead of the O(1) a proper queue implementation should guarantee, exactly mirroring the array-shifting cost issue covered for stacks/arrays in earlier modules
shift() only works on arrays containing strings, not numbers
shift() is deprecated and no longer available in JavaScript
theory_mcq.explanation: This directly parallels the L1-M02/L4-M01 principle: shift() removes from the FRONT of an array, requiring every subsequent element to move left by one position to maintain contiguity — this O(n) cost is exactly why the lesson introduces the head-pointer-based Queue class as the efficient alternative.

theory_mcq.question: Why is FIFO ordering specifically what makes BFS (breadth-first search) correctly find SHORTEST paths in level-order traversal?
options: FIFO has no actual connection to shortest paths; this is a coincidence

Because a queue processes nodes in the EXACT order they were discovered, all nodes at the CURRENT level/distance are guaranteed to be fully processed BEFORE any node at the NEXT level/distance is even examined — this strict 'finish near things before exploring far things' ordering is precisely what guarantees BFS explores nodes in increasing order of distance from the start, finding the shortest path
BFS would work identically with a stack instead of a queue
FIFO only matters for trees, never for general graphs
theory_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's explicit framing: 'FIFO ensures Level 1 is fully processed before Level 2 begins' — since elements are dequeued in the same order they were enqueued, a queue guarantees all same-distance nodes are explored together before moving farther away, which is the structural property that makes BFS optimal for shortest-path problems on unweighted graphs.

logic_mcq.question: Trace the lesson's efficient Queue: `enqueue('a'); enqueue('b'); enqueue('c'); front();` What is returned, and what are `_head` and `_tail` at that point?
options: 'c' is returned (most recently added); _head=0, _tail=3
'a' is returned (the FIRST element added, per FIFO); after three enqueues, _head is still 0 (nothing dequeued yet) and _tail is 3 (three elements added, tail advanced each time)
undefined is returned, since front() doesn't work correctly
'b' is returned, since front() always returns the middle element
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: front() reads `this._data[this._head]`, and since _head stays at 0 until a dequeue happens, front() correctly returns 'a' — the FIRST element enqueued, per FIFO. _tail has advanced to 3 after three enqueue() calls (each incrementing tail by 1), while _head remains 0.

logic_mcq.question: Continuing the same trace, after `dequeue()` is called twice (removing 'a' then 'b'), what does `q.size` return, and how is it calculated?
options: size returns 3, the total number of elements ever enqueued

size returns 1 — `get size() { return this._tail - this._head; }` computes the difference between tail (3, unchanged by dequeues) and head (now 2, after two dequeue() calls each incrementing head by 1); 3 - 2 = 1, correctly reflecting that only 'c' remains
size returns 0, since dequeue() always empties the queue
size throws an error after two dequeue calls
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: 'q.dequeue(); // 'a' — O(1)... q.dequeue(); // 'b' — O(1)... q.size; // 1' — the size getter computes tail-head (3-2=1), correctly reflecting the one remaining element ('c') without needing to physically shift any array contents.

logic_mcq.question: Why does the efficient Queue use a plain object (`this._data = {}`) rather than an array for internal storage, combined with separately tracked `_head` and `_tail` index counters?
options: Using an object has no functional benefit over an array here

Using an object with arbitrary numeric keys (rather than a true array) avoids any implicit array-index-shifting behavior — `delete this._data[this._head]` removes a single entry in O(1) without affecting neighboring keys, and incrementing `_head`/`_tail` as separate counters (rather than physically removing/inserting at array positions) is what achieves O(1) dequeue, since no other stored elements need to move when the logical 'front' advances
Objects are always faster than arrays in JavaScript for every operation
This is purely a stylistic choice with no performance implications
logic_mcq.explanation: This design choice is what enables true O(1) dequeue: by using object keys as virtual array positions and tracking _head/_tail as separate logical pointers (rather than physically shifting array contents), advancing _head++ 'removes' the front element in O(1) without touching any other stored values — directly avoiding the O(n) cost that arr.shift() would incur.

syntax_mcq.question: In `delete this._data[this._head];`, what does the `delete` keyword accomplish here, and why is it used during dequeue?
options: delete removes the entire _data object

delete removes the SPECIFIC property/key (at index this._head) from the _data object — this frees the memory associated with that one dequeued value, preventing the object from growing unboundedly as more elements are enqueued and dequeued over the queue's lifetime
delete has no effect when used on object properties
delete only works on arrays, not on plain objects
syntax_mcq.explanation: The `delete` operator removes a specific property from an object. Here, it cleans up the dequeued value's storage slot (`this._data[this._head]`) so it doesn't linger in memory indefinitely — important because without this cleanup, a long-running queue with many enqueue/dequeue cycles would otherwise accumulate stale entries in the underlying object.

theory_mcq.question: What is the 'lazy transfer' strategy in the two-stack queue implementation, and why is it called 'lazy'?
options: It means elements are randomly transferred between stacks at unpredictable times

Elements are only moved from `_in` to `_out` WHEN `_out` becomes empty AND a pop/peek operation is requested — rather than transferring immediately or eagerly after every push, the transfer is deferred ('lazy') until it's actually NEEDED, which is what allows the amortized O(1) analysis to work out favorably
It means the queue never actually transfers elements between stacks
Lazy transfer refers to using setTimeout to delay operations
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's `_transfer()` method only runs the reversal loop 'if (this._out.length === 0)' — meaning transfers are deferred (lazy) until outStack genuinely needs elements, rather than happening proactively on every operation; this deferred-until-needed strategy is exactly what produces the amortized O(1) cost analysis.

theory_mcq.question: Why does each element moving 'at most twice' (once into inStack via push, once into outStack via the lazy transfer) lead to an amortized O(1) dequeue cost, even though a single transfer operation can be O(n)?
options: It doesn't actually lead to O(1); the lesson's claim is incorrect

Across a sequence of n total push/pop operations, each individual element is moved at most twice total (one push to inStack, one push to outStack during a transfer) — so the TOTAL work across the ENTIRE sequence is bounded by 2n, which when divided by n operations gives O(1) amortized cost per operation, even though any SINGLE transfer operation might process many elements at once
This is identical to the array doubling resize analysis with no meaningful similarity
Amortized analysis doesn't apply to stack/queue implementations
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the same amortized analysis principle from L1-M01's dynamic array lesson: bounding the TOTAL work across an entire sequence of operations (here, 2n total element-moves across n operations) and dividing by the number of operations gives the amortized per-operation cost — individual operations can occasionally be expensive (a full transfer), but the AVERAGE remains O(1).

logic_mcq.question: Trace the lesson's MyQueue example precisely: push(1), push(2), push(3), pop(), push(4), pop(). What are the two pop() return values, in order?
options: 3, then 2 — reflecting LIFO order

1, then 2 — the first pop() triggers a transfer (in=[1,2,3] reverses into out=[3,2,1]), popping returns 1 (FIFO: first pushed); the second pop() (after push(4) added to a now-non-empty in=[4], with out=[3,2] remaining from before) does NOT need another transfer since out isn't empty, and pops 2 directly from out
1, then 4 — every push interferes with the previous pop sequence
Both pops return undefined since the queue malfunctions
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's own exact trace, already independently verified by direct execution: 'pop(): out empty -> transfer -> in=[], out=[3,2,1] -> pop() -> 1 FIFO... push(4): in=[4], out=[3,2]... pop(): out not empty -> pop() -> 2 FIFO (no transfer needed)' — both pop() results are 1 then 2, correctly preserving FIFO order despite the underlying two-stack mechanics.

logic_mcq.question: In `CircularQueue`, why does `get _tail()` compute `(this._head + this._size) % this._cap` rather than tracking a separate `_tail` variable directly?
options: This computation is unnecessary; a separate tracked variable would be simpler with no downside

Deriving _tail from _head, _size, and _cap (using modulo to wrap around) guarantees _tail always stays mathematically consistent with the current _head and _size — avoiding the need to separately update and synchronize a third tracked variable (which could otherwise drift out of sync with _head/_size if updated incorrectly in some code path), and the modulo operation correctly handles wrap-around when the logical tail position exceeds the buffer's physical capacity
JavaScript getters cannot use the % operator, so this is a workaround
This formula always returns 0 regardless of input values
logic_mcq.explanation: Computing _tail as a DERIVED value (rather than a separately tracked variable) eliminates an entire class of synchronization bugs, since it's mathematically guaranteed to be consistent with _head and _size at all times — the modulo operation specifically handles the circular wrap-around behavior, ensuring the computed tail position correctly 'wraps' back to the beginning of the fixed-capacity buffer when needed.

syntax_mcq.question: In `this._head = (this._head + 1) % this._cap;`, what does the modulo operation `% this._cap` accomplish for a circular buffer?
options: It has no effect; this is equivalent to just `this._head + 1`

It WRAPS the incremented head index back to 0 once it would exceed the buffer's capacity — for example, if _cap is 5 and _head was at index 4 (the last valid index), incrementing normally would give 5 (out of bounds), but `5 % 5` correctly wraps back to 0, treating the buffer as logically circular rather than linear
It always resets _head to 0 regardless of the current value
It only works correctly when _cap is an even number
syntax_mcq.explanation: The modulo operation is what makes the buffer 'circular': once the head index would advance past the last valid position (cap-1), the modulo wraps it back to 0, reusing the buffer's space from the beginning rather than requiring unbounded growth — this is the defining mechanism of a circular/ring buffer.

theory_mcq.question: What is the defining invariant of a 'monotonic stack', and how is this invariant maintained?
options: A monotonic stack is just a regular stack with a different name

A monotonic stack always remains SORTED (either entirely increasing or entirely decreasing) at every point during execution — this invariant is maintained by POPPING elements that would violate the sort order BEFORE pushing the new element, ensuring the stack's order property never breaks
A monotonic stack can only hold exactly one type of value
A monotonic stack automatically sorts itself using a built-in sort() call after every push
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's core definition: 'stack that is always sorted (increasing or decreasing)' — maintained via 'invariant maintenance: pop elements that violate the order' BEFORE the new element is pushed, which is exactly the while-loop pattern shown in nextGreaterElement.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson's proof that 'each element is pushed and popped at most once' establish O(n) time complexity for the Next Greater Element algorithm, despite the nested while-loop-inside-a-for-loop structure?
options: The nested loop structure actually makes this O(n²), and the lesson's claim is wrong

Even though there's a while loop nested inside a for loop (which often suggests O(n²)), the TOTAL number of push and pop operations across the ENTIRE execution is bounded by 2n (each of the n elements is pushed exactly once, and popped AT MOST once) — this means the COMBINED work across all iterations of the while loop, summed across the entire outer for loop, is still bounded by O(n), not O(n) per outer iteration
The algorithm doesn't actually use a while loop internally
O(n) only applies when the input array is already sorted
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the same amortized-style argument used for sliding windows (L1-M02): nested loop SHAPE doesn't automatically mean O(n²) — what matters is the TOTAL work across the entire execution. Since each element can only be pushed once and popped once (2n total operations across the whole run, not per outer iteration), the overall complexity is O(n).

logic_mcq.question: Trace `nextGreaterElement([2,1,2,4,3])` per the lesson's own worked example, focusing specifically on what happens at i=3 (value 4). Which indices get popped, and what result values do they receive?
options: No indices are popped at i=3

Two indices are popped at i=3: first index 2 (value 2, since 2 < 4) gets result[2]=4, then index 0 (value 2, since 2 < 4) gets result[0]=4 — both popped because nums[3]=4 is greater than both, processed in LIFO order from the stack
Only index 0 is popped at i=3
All four previous indices are popped simultaneously
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: 'i=3: nums[2]=2 < nums[3]=4 -> pop 2, result[2]=4. nums[0]=2 < nums[3]=4 -> pop 0, result[0]=4. stack empty -> push 3' — the while loop continues popping as long as the stack top's value is smaller than the current value, processing index 2 first (it was pushed more recently, LIFO), then index 0.

logic_mcq.question: In the final trace result `[4, 2, 4, -1, -1]` for input `[2,1,2,4,3]`, why do the last two positions (indices 3 and 4, values 4 and 3) both receive -1?
options: This is an error; they should receive actual values

Indices 3 and 4 are the LAST two elements remaining in the stack at the end of the algorithm's execution — since no element AFTER them in the array was ever large enough to trigger a pop for them (4 is the maximum value in the array, and nothing follows 3 that's larger than 3), they never get assigned a 'next greater element' and retain their default value of -1, correctly indicating no greater element exists to their right
Indices 3 and 4 represent invalid array positions
The algorithm always assigns -1 to the last two elements regardless of their values
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: 'End: indices 3,4 remain -> result[3]=result[4]=-1' — the result array is initialized to -1 by default, and only OVERWRITTEN when an element is popped during the algorithm; elements remaining on the stack at the very end (here, indices 3 and 4) never had a qualifying 'next greater' element appear, so their -1 default correctly persists.

syntax_mcq.question: In `while (stack.length > 0 && nums[stack[stack.length - 1]] < nums[i])`, why does the stack store INDICES rather than the actual VALUES from nums?
options: Storing indices is purely a stylistic preference with no functional benefit

Storing indices allows the algorithm to know WHERE in the result array to write the answer (result[idx] = nums[i]) when a match is found — if only VALUES were stored, the algorithm would lose track of which array POSITION each value came from, making it impossible to correctly populate the position-indexed result array, especially when duplicate values exist in the input
JavaScript arrays cannot store numeric values directly in a stack
Storing indices makes the comparison nums[stack[top]] < nums[i] run faster than storing values directly
syntax_mcq.explanation: Storing indices (rather than raw values) is essential because the algorithm needs to know WHICH POSITION in the result array to update once a match is found — `result[idx] = nums[i]` requires the original index, and this is especially important when the input contains DUPLICATE values, where storing only the value would make it ambiguous which occurrence's result should be updated.

theory_mcq.question: How does Daily Temperatures differ from the basic Next Greater Element problem in terms of WHAT VALUE gets stored in the result, even though both use the same monotonic decreasing stack technique?
options: There is no difference; they are identical problems

Next Greater Element stores the ACTUAL VALUE of the next greater element (e.g., result[idx] = nums[i]), while Daily Temperatures stores the DISTANCE (number of days/positions) between the current index and the index that triggered the pop (result[prevDay] = i - prevDay) — the underlying monotonic stack mechanics are identical, but what gets recorded at each pop differs

Daily Temperatures only works on arrays of exactly 8 elements
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's explicit comparison: 'Comparing to Next Greater Element I: value vs distance' — both problems use the identical monotonic decreasing stack mechanics (pop when current beats stack top), but Next Greater Element records the VALUE that beat the popped element, while Daily Temperatures records the INDEX DISTANCE (i - prevDay) between them.

theory_mcq.question: Why do indices remaining in the stack at the very end of `dailyTemperatures` correctly default to a result of 0, rather than -1 or any other value?
options: 0 is an arbitrary, meaningless default with no connection to the problem

The problem asks 'how many days must you wait for a warmer temperature' — if NO warmer day ever follows a given day (it remains in the stack until the array ends), the correct answer is that you wait 0 MORE days (i.e., there is no day to wait for), which is semantically different from Next Greater Element's -1 (meaning 'no such element exists') but serves the same role: the default value for 'no qualifying answer was found'
0 indicates an error occurred during processing
0 means the temperature was exactly 0 degrees
theory_mcq.explanation: The result array represents 'days to wait', and 0 is the semantically correct default for 'never gets warmer' (you wait 0 additional days, since there's nothing to wait for) — this mirrors how Next Greater Element uses -1 as its 'no answer' default, but each problem chooses the default value appropriate to what its result actually represents.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `dailyTemperatures([73,74,75,71,69,72,76,73])` per the lesson's own worked example, focusing on i=5 (temperature 72). Which indices get popped, and what result values do they receive?
options: No indices are popped at i=5

Two indices are popped at i=5: index 4 (temp 69, since 69<72) receives result[4]=5-4=1, then index 3 (temp 71, since 71<72) receives result[3]=5-3=2 — both popped in LIFO order since 72 is warmer than both
Only index 2 is popped at i=5
All prior indices are popped simultaneously at i=5
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: 'i=5 (72): 72>69 -> pop 4, result[4]=5-4=1. 72>71 -> pop 3, result[3]=5-3=2. 72<75, push' — the while loop pops index 4 first (most recently pushed, LIFO), then index 3, both because their temperatures (69, 71) are less than the current day's temperature (72).

logic_mcq.question: In the final result `[1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]` for `[73,74,75,71,69,72,76,73]`, why does index 2 (temperature 75) get the value 4 specifically (waiting 4 days for a warmer temperature)?
options: This is a calculation error; the correct value should be different

Index 2 (temp 75) is popped at i=6 (temp 76, the first day warmer than 75) — the distance calculation is i - prevDay = 6 - 2 = 4, meaning from day index 2, you must wait exactly 4 days (until day index 6) to find a warmer temperature (76 > 75)
Index 2 always receives a fixed value of 4 regardless of the actual data
The value 4 represents the temperature difference (76-75=1, doubled somehow)
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: 'i=6 (76): 76>72 -> pop 5... 76>75 -> pop 2, result[2]=6-2=4' — index 2's temperature (75) is finally exceeded at index 6 (76), and the distance formula i-prevDay=6-2=4 correctly computes that 4 days must pass (from day 2 to day 6) before a warmer temperature arrives.

syntax_mcq.question: In `result[prevDay] = i - prevDay;`, what does this expression compute, and why is it `i - prevDay` rather than `prevDay - i`?
options: It computes the temperature difference between the two days

It computes the NUMBER OF DAYS (the distance in array positions) between prevDay (the earlier day being resolved) and i (the current day that's warmer) — since i is always GREATER than prevDay (the current index always comes after the day it resolves, as the stack only holds indices from earlier processing), `i - prevDay` correctly produces a POSITIVE day-count; `prevDay - i` would incorrectly produce a negative number
It computes a random value with no real meaning
It always evaluates to exactly 1
syntax_mcq.explanation: Since `prevDay` was pushed onto the stack at an EARLIER point in the loop (a smaller index) and `i` is the CURRENT (later, larger) index, `i - prevDay` is guaranteed to be positive and correctly represents 'how many days passed between the earlier day and the day that finally proved warmer' — reversing the subtraction would produce an incorrect negative value.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson use a MONOTONIC INCREASING stack for Largest Rectangle in Histogram, in contrast to the monotonic DECREASING stack used for Next Greater Element and Daily Temperatures?
options: The choice between increasing and decreasing is arbitrary with no actual reason

The key insight is 'a bar limits the height of any rectangle it is part of' — by maintaining an INCREASING stack (popping when the CURRENT bar is SHORTER than the stack top), each popped bar represents the limiting (shortest) height for a rectangle whose width can now be precisely calculated, since we've just found both the bar that ends its potential rectangle on the right (current bar, shorter) and can determine the left boundary from what remains on the stack
Increasing stacks are always faster than decreasing stacks
This problem doesn't actually use a monotonic stack at all
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's stated key insight directly explains this: when a SHORTER bar arrives, every TALLER bar on the stack can no longer extend its rectangle rightward past this point — so each such taller bar's MAXIMUM possible rectangle area can now be finalized and computed, which is exactly why popping happens specifically when a SHORTER (height-limiting) bar is encountered, requiring the stack to track bars in increasing order.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson append a sentinel value of 0 to the end of the heights array before processing?
options: The sentinel has no functional purpose; it's purely decorative

Without the sentinel, any bars still remaining on the stack at the natural END of the array would never get popped (and thus their potential rectangles would never be computed) — appending a height-0 sentinel guarantees that EVERY remaining bar on the stack will be popped (since 0 is shorter than any actual bar height), forcing the algorithm to correctly compute and consider every bar's maximum rectangle before the function returns
The sentinel changes the input array's actual histogram shape
The sentinel is required by JavaScript syntax for array operations
theory_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's explicit explanation: 'Sentinel value: append height 0 to force all pops at the end' — without this, bars remaining on the stack when the loop naturally ends would never trigger the pop-and-compute-area logic, potentially missing the true maximum if the largest rectangle involves one of those un-popped bars.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `largestRectangleArea([2,1,5,6,2,3])` per the lesson's own worked example, focusing on i=4 (height 2, with sentinel appended). Which bars get popped, and what areas are computed?
options: No bars are popped at i=4

Two bars are popped at i=4: first index 3 (height 6) with width=4-2-1=1 giving area=6, then index 2 (height 5) with width=4-1-1=2 giving area=10 — both popped because the current height (2) is less than both, with widths computed using the NEW stack top after each respective pop
Only index 3 is popped, with an area of 6
All bars are popped simultaneously with a single combined area calculation
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: 'i=4 (h=2): 2<6 -> pop 3, h=6, top=2 -> w=4-2-1=1, area=6. 2<5 -> pop 2, h=5, top=1 -> w=4-1-1=2, area=10' — the while loop pops index 3 first (LIFO), computing width using the stack's new top (index 2) AFTER that pop, then continues popping index 2, computing width using the NEXT new top (index 1) after THAT pop.

logic_mcq.question: Why does the width formula use `i - stack[stack.length-1] - 1` (the NEW stack top AFTER popping) rather than the OLD stack top from before the pop?
options: Either the old or new top would give the identical width; this distinction doesn't matter

The just-popped bar's rectangle is bounded on the LEFT by whatever bar remains JUST BELOW it on the stack (after removal) — that REMAINING bar represents the nearest bar to the left that is SHORTER than the popped bar (since the stack maintains increasing order, everything below the popped bar must be shorter), correctly establishing the left boundary of the popped bar's maximal rectangle; the OLD top (the bar that was just removed) is no longer relevant to this calculation since it's the bar whose area is being computed, not a boundary
Using the old top would cause a syntax error
The formula doesn't actually use the stack top at all
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the precise reasoning behind the width formula: after popping the limiting (just-removed) bar, the bar now exposed at the new stack top is the nearest SHORTER bar to its left (guaranteed by the monotonic increasing invariant) — this defines exactly how far the popped bar's rectangle could extend leftward, while the current index i defines how far right it extends (up to, but not including, i, since the bar AT i is what triggered the pop by being too short).

logic_mcq.question: What is the maximum area found across the entire trace of `largestRectangleArea([2,1,5,6,2,3])`, and at which step is it achieved?
options: Maximum area is 6, found at i=4 when popping index 3

Maximum area is 10, found at i=4 when popping index 2 (height 5, width 2) — this remains the maximum through the rest of the trace, since the subsequent areas computed at the sentinel step (i=6: areas 3, 8, 6) are all smaller than 10
Maximum area is 8, found at the very end
Maximum area is 2, the smallest bar height in the array
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's final stated result: 'maxArea = 10' — this value is established at i=4 (height=5, width=4-1-1=2, area=10) and remains the maximum throughout the rest of the trace, since the sentinel-triggered pops at i=6 produce smaller areas (3, 8, and 6 respectively), none of which exceed 10.

syntax_mcq.question: In `const width = stack.length === 0 ? i : i - stack[stack.length - 1] - 1;`, why does the width calculation differ when the stack becomes EMPTY after a pop, compared to when elements remain?
options: There's no actual difference; both branches compute the same thing

If the stack is EMPTY after popping (meaning the just-popped bar was the SHORTEST bar seen so far, with nothing shorter to its left within the array), its rectangle can extend all the way back to index 0 — so width is simply `i` (the full span from the start up to but not including the current index); if elements REMAIN on the stack, the rectangle is bounded on the left by the new top, so the formula `i - stack[top] - 1` correctly excludes that boundary bar from the width
The empty-stack case always returns a width of 0
This ternary expression contains a bug and should always use the same formula
syntax_mcq.explanation: An empty stack after popping means there's no bar to the left that's shorter than the just-popped bar within the processed range — so its rectangle could theoretically span from index 0 all the way to (but not including) the current index i, giving width=i; when bars remain, the new top establishes a concrete left boundary, requiring the more complex `i - stack[top] - 1` formula to exclude that boundary position from the width count.

coding_challenges.title: Largest Rectangle Solver with Step-by-Step Area Tracer
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Implement Largest Rectangle in Histogram matching the lesson exactly, then build a tracer version that records every intermediate area computed during execution, useful for understanding and debugging the algorithm's step-by-step behavior.
requirements: Implement `largestRectangleAreaImpl(heights)` matching the lesson's sentinel + monotonic increasing stack approach exactly

Implement `largestRectangleAreaTraced(heights)` returning `{ maxArea, allAreasComputed }` where allAreasComputed is an array listing every individual area value computed during the entire execution (in the order they were computed), useful for verifying the algorithm explores all necessary candidate rectangles
coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: largestRectangleAreaImpl: O(n) time, O(n) space (same once-pushed-once-popped proof as the other monotonic stack algorithms). largestRectangleAreaTraced: O(n) time, O(n) space, with the additional allAreasComputed array also bounded by O(n) entries.

hints.text: largestRectangleAreaImpl should match the lesson's implementation exactly, including the sentinel-appending step.
largestRectangleAreaTraced is identical logic, just push each computed area into a tracking array before/after updating maxArea.
Remember the width formula's two branches: stack.length===0 after popping means width=i (extends to the start); otherwise width=i-stack[top]-1 (bounded by the new top).

theory_mcq.question: What recognition signals does the lesson give for choosing STACK versus QUEUE versus MONOTONIC STACK?
options: There are no distinguishing signals; the choice is always arbitrary
Stack signals: 'nested', 'matching', 'undo', 'DFS'. Queue signals: 'level by level', 'BFS', 'in order received'. Monotonic stack signals: 'next greater/smaller', 'span', 'histogram'
All three data structures are used interchangeably for every problem

theory_mcq.explanation: These are the lesson's exact stated recognition signals for each of the three sub-categories — matching language patterns in a problem statement to the underlying data structure is the core skill this lesson aims to build, mirroring the pattern-recognition approach from earlier modules' final lessons.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson explicitly note that 'recursion and sorting use stacks implicitly' as a bridge to Module 5, even though those topics don't involve an explicit Stack class?
options: This statement is incorrect; recursion has no relationship to stacks

Even when a programmer doesn't manually create a Stack object, the underlying CALL STACK mechanism (covered in L1-M01) IS a stack — every recursive function call implicitly uses LIFO call-stack behavior, meaning the conceptual understanding built in this module (stack mechanics, LIFO ordering) transfers directly to understanding recursion's behavior, even without an explicit data structure being instantiated
Sorting algorithms always require manually building a Stack class
This statement only applies to languages other than JavaScript
theory_mcq.explanation: This connects back to L1-M01's recursion lesson: the call stack that manages function calls IS a stack (LIFO), even though no programmer-visible Stack object is created — understanding stack mechanics from this module gives a deeper, more concrete mental model for WHY recursion behaves the way it does (e.g., why deeply nested recursive calls can cause a 'stack overflow', a term this module's L1 also covered).

logic_mcq.question: A problem states: 'Find the span of stock prices, where span[i] is the number of consecutive days (ending at day i) where the price was less than or equal to today's price.' Applying the lesson's decision tree, which category applies, and why?

None of the three categories apply to this problem

logic_mcq.question: Per the lesson's Module 4 problem map, 'Implement Queue using Stacks' (#232) and 'Implement Stack using Queues' (#225) are both marked `blind75: false`, unlike most other problems in the list. It means these problems are duplicates of other Blind75 problems
It means the Blind75 flag is broken for these two specific entries

syntax_mcq.question: In `console.log('Module 4 Blind 75 problems:', module4_problems.filter(p => p.blind75).length);`, what does `.filter(p => p.blind75)` accomplish?

coding_challenges.title: Capstone Project: Stack/Queue Pattern Classifier and Multi-Solver
